headline: Anthropic's debut fails to lift the AI trade and all 11 sectors fall; energy holds up best, discretionary and communication services lead the slide
summary: SPY fell 2.0% on Thursday and the equal-weight RSP 1.8%, a sixth straight loss for the S&P 500; over the past month SPY is down 7.4% and RSP 2.3%. Every sector fell: energy lost least (−0.7%), then utilities (−1.2%) and staples (−1.4%), while discretionary (−2.8%), communication services (−2.7%) and materials (−2.1%) fell most. Over the month staples (+3.2%), utilities (+2.4%) and real estate (+1.9%) lead, and tech (−14.8%), energy (−10.7%) and communication services (−5.7%) lag. The trigger was the AI complex reversing after Anthropic began trading, with a short report on AMD, more managed-care selling and a soft jobs and Philly Fed print that only nudged the 10-year down to 5.05%.
drivers: The AI trade reverses after Anthropic's debut

Anthropic opened 34% above its $83 IPO price but closed +17.1% as the early AI bounce faded: Nvidia went from +4.7% to −3.3% and AMD fell 7.7% on a Hunterbrook short report, leaving XLK −1.9%. Money raised for the record IPO had to come from somewhere, and Amazon (about −2.7%) and Alphabet (−3.5%), the two biggest outside holders, were sold, which put XLY (−2.8%) and XLC (−2.7%) at the bottom.

Health care fell 2.0% as UnitedHealth lost another 5.6% on the Medicare Advantage audit proposal, and Walmart slipped about 1% despite a beat and its third guidance raise of the year; staples still fell 1.4%. Williams-Sonoma's roughly 15% drop added to discretionary's losses. More than 90% of S&P 500 members fell and the VIX rose 15.8% to 28.44.
Energy loses least as oil steadies

WTI was flat at $83.21 as Iranian claims of tankers hitting mines near Hormuz offset surplus worries, so XLE fell only 0.7%. It is still −13.0% month to date with RSI 21, the most oversold reading on the page.

Continuing jobless claims jumped to a ten-week high of 1.763m and the Philly Fed index slowed to 6.3, but the 10-year eased only about 1bp to 5.05% with a December hike almost fully priced. Financials fell 1.5% and closed below their 50-day average.
rotation: Materials moved from Leading to Weakening since the last recap: its 3-month relative strength turned negative (−1.0 points) with the price 3.0% below its 200-day. That leaves seven sectors in Leading (staples, utilities, health care, financials, real estate, discretionary and industrials), energy and materials in Weakening, communication services in Improving and tech in Lagging. Inside Leading the defensives are the strongest, with staples at +11.5 points and health care at +8.3, though health care is now only 0.7% above its 50-day with RSI 37. Energy's relative strength is down to +2.5 points but it is falling less than SPY, while tech is at −6.0 points and 13.2% below its 50-day. The defensive rotation ends when XLK reclaims its 50-day average with creations continuing and staples and utilities start to lose relative strength; Thursday's reversal pushed that further out.
flows: State Street flows to Nov 18 show ETF holders still buying tech into the slide: XLK took in $595m in a week (0.5% of assets), $2.05bn in a month (1.9%) and $3.59bn over 3 months (3.3%) while its price fell 14.8% in a month. The heaviest selling is in the havens that are rallying: utilities lost $1.75bn in a month (7.5% of assets) and staples $784m (5.3%) despite monthly gains of 2.4% and 3.2%, so the defensive bid looks like institutional positioning that the ETF holders are fading. Financials keep bleeding: −$308m in a week, −$1.14bn in a month (2.2%) and −$3.13bn over 3 months (6.0%), and energy lost $501m in a week (1.3%), its fastest pace on the page. Materials took in $325m in a month (4.0% of assets) and health care $313m (0.7%), though health care saw $189m leave in the latest week. For scale, SPY took in $8.70bn in the week (1.1% of its $0.78tn) and $5.68bn over the month, so broad beta is being bought while sector money rotates.
model: The six-factor model still ranks energy first, with its score edging up to 77 from 75; health care is second (64, down from 68), then staples (54), materials (53), tech (52) and financials (51). Real estate (48) and discretionary (44) follow, utilities rose to ninth (39) past industrials (37), and communication services stays last (31). Energy's lead rests on +54% 12-1 month momentum, a 12.2x forward P/E and 151% Q3 earnings growth, while its 1-month flows (−2.0% of assets) and RSI 21 point the other way, so I stay neutral. Utilities and staples are held back by the worst flow scores (−7.5% and −5.3% of assets). I differ on tech, where 1.9% inflows and oversold readings make me more constructive than fifth, and I have now cut financials to neutral, in line with the model's mid-table rank, after the 50-day break.
weightsSrc: Schwab Center for Financial Research, as of Oct 2, 2026; rolled forward by each sector ETF's price change

XLV.view: Health care fell 2.0% as UnitedHealth dropped another 5.6% on the Medicare Advantage audit proposal, so the sector traded with the market rather than as a haven; XLV is −0.8% over a month. Pharma and tools carry less of this risk, and BofA's November survey shows fund managers lifting their health care overweight to a net 34% from 23%. That positioning support is why I keep the overweight despite the managed-care drag.
XLV.modelView: Second (64, down from 68): +8.3 points of 3-month relative strength and the strongest trend (11.0% above the 200-day), with 1-month inflows of 0.7% of assets. Weak spots are 9% Q3 earnings growth, RSI 37 and $189m of outflows in the latest week.
XLV.trade: Hold the overweight through pharma and tools; cut to neutral on a close below the 50-day average (now just 0.7% below the price), and avoid managed care until the CRUSH rule's comment period (to Jan 19) clarifies the audit exposure.
XLV.risk: The audit rule spreading to a wider Medicare Advantage squeeze; crowded defensive positioning unwinding if tech rebounds.

XLF.view: Cut to neutral from overweight: XLF fell 1.5% on Thursday and closed 0.6% below its 50-day average, the trigger set in the last recap, and redemptions keep building ($3.13bn over 3 months). A 10-year above 5% still supports bank margins and at 15.1x forward earnings the sector is cheap, but a December hike and private-credit worries are weighing on the group.
XLF.modelView: Sixth (51): +3.3 points of 3-month relative strength and 3.4% above the 200-day, held back by flows ($1.14bn out in a month, 2.2% of assets) and modest 12-1 month momentum (+11%).
XLF.trade: Neutral; move back to overweight on a close above the 50-day average with weekly redemptions stopping, and prefer large money-centre banks and brokers over regionals.
XLF.risk: Private-credit or commercial real estate losses; a flatter curve if the Fed hikes 50bp.

XLK.view: Tech fell 1.9% as the AI bounce on Anthropic's debut reversed: Nvidia closed −3.3% and AMD −7.7% on a short report, while Palo Alto (+6.4%) and CrowdStrike gained. BofA's November survey shows managers cut tech to a net 12% overweight from 37%, the biggest drop since 2006; the survey's best entry points have come when tech goes underweight, which has not happened yet. XLK is −14.8% over a month with RSI 32, earned 69% Q3 earnings growth and trades below the market multiple.
XLK.modelView: Fifth (52): the second-best 12-1 month momentum (+36%), a strong valuation score and 1-month inflows of 1.9% of assets offset the worst 3-month relative strength (−6.0 points) and a price 6.0% below the 200-day.
XLK.trade: Keep building towards benchmark in thirds: the first tranche is in; the second on a close back above the 50-day average (13.2% above), the third on a retest of the low that holds.
XLK.risk: ETF dip-buyers capitulating if Nvidia and AMD keep falling; a hyperscaler capex cut, which 52% of BofA's surveyed managers expect within six months.

XLP.view: Staples fell 1.4% on Thursday but are +3.2% over the month as a haven. Walmart beat and raised its full-year outlook for the third time but slipped about 1%, a sign that defensive leaders are priced for good news. At 23.7x forward earnings the sector costs about 30% more than the market, and ETF holders are selling ($784m out in a month).
XLP.modelView: Third (54, down from 59): the strongest 3-month relative strength (+11.5 points) and trend (6.7% above the 200-day), with a weak valuation score and the second-worst flow score (−5.3% of assets in a month).
XLP.trade: Neutral; keep trimming into haven rallies and rotate into pharma within health care.
XLP.risk: A deeper growth scare would extend the defensive bid.

XLE.view: Energy fell least on Thursday (−0.7%) as WTI held $83.21, steadied by Iranian claims of tanker incidents near Hormuz against surplus worries. It is the cheapest sector (12.2x) with the fastest earnings growth (151% in Q3 per FactSet), but XLE is −13.0% month to date and RSI 21, and ETF holders pulled $501m in a week. Crude still has not regained the mid-$80s.
XLE.modelView: First in the model (77, up from 75): valuation, earnings and 12-1 month momentum (+54%) carry it, while price (−10.7% in a month), flows (−2.0% of assets) and the Weakening quadrant point the other way, which is why I don't follow the model's overweight.
XLE.trade: Neutral; don't add until WTI regains $85 and XLE recloses above its 50-day average (now 6.0% below it); oversold readings alone are not a signal.
XLE.risk: Further surplus-driven oil weakness; Gulf escalation is the upside risk.

XLB.view: Materials fell 2.1% as gold dropped about 2.7% and silver almost 5% on hike pricing and a dollar near a 19-month high. XLB moved into the Weakening quadrant and is 3.0% below its 200-day, though Q3 earnings grew about 30% (FactSet). ETF buyers are still adding, with $325m in a month.
XLB.modelView: Fourth (53, up from 52): 1-month inflows of 4.0% of assets, the best flow score on the page, and +22% 12-1 month momentum, against −1.0 points of 3-month relative strength and a price 3.0% below the 200-day.
XLB.trade: Neutral; wait for a close back above the 200-day before adding, and prefer data-center materials over miners while metals break down.
XLB.risk: A stronger dollar and slower China demand.

XLC.view: Communication services fell 2.7% as Alphabet dropped 3.5%, with investors likely selling it to fund Anthropic shares even as the IPO put a higher value on its stake. The sector is −11.9% this year and 7.9% below its 200-day as investors question returns on AI spending, though earnings grew about 18% in Q3 and it trades at about 18x forward earnings. Wells Fargo is overweight for 2027.
XLC.modelView: Last (31): flat 12-1 month momentum (−1%), 7.9% below the 200-day and $800m of outflows in a month (3.7% of assets). Valuation and earnings are the positives, and it stays in Improving on the rotation map.
XLC.trade: Neutral; a bounce candidate if tech turns, but it needs to reclaim its 200-day average first.
XLC.risk: More capex without matching revenue; advertising slowing if the consumer weakens.

XLI.view: Industrials fell 2.1% and are −10.2% over three months as the AI-power equipment trade unwound and growth data softened (Philly Fed 6.3 from 20.9). At 22.5x forward earnings they trade at a premium to the market. Morgan Stanley picks the sector for 2027, while Wells Fargo has it at equal weight.
XLI.modelView: Tenth (37), down one place: −4.0 points of 3-month relative strength, 6.6% below the 200-day and a poor valuation score. Flows are small: $114m in over a month, $182m out in the latest week.
XLI.trade: Underweight; keep aerospace and defence, and revisit electrical equipment only on a close back above the 200-day.
XLI.risk: A fast AI-capex rebound would lift the electrical-equipment names first.

XLY.view: Discretionary was the worst sector on Thursday (−2.8%): Amazon fell about 2.7% as money moved into Anthropic, and Williams-Sonoma dropped about 15% on a revenue miss. Walmart's raised outlook did not help the group. At 25.1x forward earnings it is the most expensive sector and −2.4% this year; BofA's survey shows managers adding to the consumer sectors from an underweight.
XLY.modelView: Eighth (44): +4.7 points of 3-month relative strength and 0.7% above the 200-day, but weak 12-1 month momentum (+4%) and the weakest valuation score; $100m of creations in a month.
XLY.trade: Underweight; move to neutral only if Black Friday and Cyber Monday data confirm spending and XLY holds its 200-day average.
XLY.risk: A strong holiday season or an Amazon-led re-rating forcing the move to neutral sooner.

XLU.view: Utilities fell 1.2% on Thursday, the second-smallest loss, and are +2.4% over the month as a haven. But ETF holders keep selling into strength: $219m out in a week and $1.75bn in a month. Morgan Stanley is overweight on power demand; a December hike caps the bond-proxy bid.
XLU.modelView: Ninth (39, up from tenth): +7.6 points of 3-month relative strength, but weak 12-1 month momentum (−3%) and the worst flow score (−7.5% of assets in a month); RSI 44 and 2.0% below the 200-day.
XLU.trade: Underweight; use haven bounces to reduce.
XLU.risk: A bond rally if the Fed turns dovish, or a sharper risk-off move.

XLRE.view: Real estate fell 1.7% on Thursday but is +1.9% over the month. It is the most rate-sensitive sector with a December hike almost fully priced, and office and retail still face refinancing at much higher rates.
XLRE.modelView: Seventh (48): +2.2 points of relative strength, the best 20-day money flow (CMF +0.06) and $75m of creations in a month, but weak 12-1 month momentum (+7%) and no valuation input.
XLRE.trade: Underweight the sector; prefer data-center and health-care REITs if exposure is needed.
XLRE.risk: A fall in long yields would spark a sharp short-covering rally.
